analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card interest at 10% has had no hearing or vote since it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on February 4, 2025, with four senators backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for credit card companies to charge more than 10% annual interest on credit card borrowing, with all fees counted toward that limit, through January 1, 2031. Cardholders who get overcharged could sue to recover every dollar of interest, finance charges, or fees, and lenders who knowingly violate the cap would forfeit all interest on the debt. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry credit card balances month to month would see interest charges cut by more than half from rates that commonly run above 20%. Cardholders who are overcharged could recover all interest and fees in court, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and Federal Trade Commission could enforce the cap. States could keep or add stronger protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households carrying month-to-month credit card debt

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 10%, inclusive of all finance charges, cutting interest costs by more than half from rates that commonly run above 20%.
Bars lenders from dodging the cap by loading costs into fees: any fees that are not counted as finance charges cannot exceed the total finance charges on the account.

Gives overcharged cardholders a private right of action to recover every dollar of interest, finance charges, or fees paid within two years, and makes knowing violators forfeit the entire interest on the debt.
Makes violations enforceable by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission under the Truth in Lending Act, and explicitly preserves stronger state consumer protections.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — mainly large banks — would lose the difference between current rates above 20% and the 10% cap, and would face forfeiture of all interest plus private lawsuits for knowing violations. Some borrowers with poor credit could see tighter access to cards if lenders stop lending to them rather than lend at the capped rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers, mainly large banks

drawbacks.text: The cap is temporary: it disappears on January 1, 2031, so any relief lasts only until the sunset unless Congress extends it.

A flat 10% cap leaves lenders no way to charge more for riskier borrowers, so they may respond by denying cards or cutting credit limits for people with low credit scores rather than lending at the capped rate.
Fees that are not classified as finance charges can still be charged up to the total amount of finance charges, leaving lenders a partial path to recoup revenue outside the cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households who carry a balance, a 10% cap would dramatically cut interest costs and create court-enforceable ways to recover overcharges — a large, direct benefit. The costs fall mainly on card issuers' revenue, though a hard cap could also shrink credit access for the riskiest borrowers and reduce card rewards funded by interest income. The 2031 sunset limits how long any downside could run, and the bill leaves stronger state laws intact. On balance, the help to indebted households outweighs the costs, though the bill does nothing for borrowers who may lose access to credit entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in February 2025 and has sat there ever since with no hearing, vote, or further action.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 4, 2025, joined from the start by Republican Senator Josh Hawley.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Three senators cosponsored — one Republican and two Democrats — bringing total support to four of 100 senators.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, which continue charging rates far above 10% on household balances while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers charging above-20% rates

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card interest at 10% and pursued cosponsors.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders as the bill's Republican cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Two Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors after introduction.

for.name: Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: As a candidate in 2024, publicly called for a temporary 10% cap on credit card interest rates, the same policy this bill would enact.

against.name: Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which has seen no committee action since February 2025.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed interest rate caps, arguing they would reduce revenue and restrict credit access for riskier borrowers.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — an independent lead sponsor, one Republican, and two Democrats — but no committee or floor vote has occurred, so how the Senate as a whole would split is unknown.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (major banks and card companies)
industries.note: A 10% cap inclusive of all finance charges would cut interest revenue on balances that currently carry rates commonly above 20%. Knowing violations would trigger forfeiture of the entire interest on the debt plus private lawsuits and federal enforcement.

industries.industry: Credit unions and community banks that issue cards
industries.note: They issue credit cards at high rates and would face the same cap and penalties. Smaller lenders have historically argued that flat caps leave them unable to price for risk, which could shrink credit for marginal borrowers — a concern that partly runs alongside, not against, borrowers' interests.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress runs through early January 2027. With four sponsors and no committee action roughly a year after introduction, the most likely path is that the bill dies in the Banking Committee without a vote, as interest-rate cap proposals have in past Congresses. It could advance only if the committee chair schedules it or if leadership attaches it to larger legislation.
